slots.label: Paragraph 1
slots.default: The idea that Macs do not get malware is comfortably out of date. macOS is actively targeted, most commonly by information stealers dressed up as legitimate installers or browser downloads, which go after saved passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets. The delivery method is usually a person being persuaded to run something, which is exactly why endpoint protection and user awareness both matter.

slots.label: List item 1
slots.default: Managed endpoint protection for macOS with central alerting

slots.label: List item 2
slots.default: FileVault full-disk encryption enforced and key escrow held

slots.label: List item 3
slots.default: macOS and third-party app patching on a schedule

slots.label: List item 4
slots.default: Administrator rights controlled rather than default

slots.label: List item 6
slots.default: Remote lock and wipe for lost or stolen devices

slots.label: Heading 2
slots.default: What macOS already does for you

slots.label: Paragraph 3
slots.default: macOS does ship with some solid defences of its own. Gatekeeper and notarisation check what is allowed to run, XProtect removes known malicious software, and System Integrity Protection stops much of the operating system being tampered with. Those are a solid floor, not a managed security programme. None of them tell you that a device has stopped receiving updates, that encryption was switched off, or that someone has been granted admin rights they should not have.

slots.label: Heading 3
slots.default: Cyber Essentials applies to Macs too

slots.label: Paragraph 4
slots.default: The five Cyber Essentials controls apply to Macs exactly as they apply to Windows: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. We hold Cyber Essentials certification ourselves and take clients through it, and Macs are assessed alongside everything else rather than quietly left out of scope.
